name: On-Chain Forensics
title: On-Chain Forensics
answer: On-chain forensics is the practice of examining blockchain transaction records to trace the movement of digital assets, attribute addresses to real-world entities, and reconstruct financial activity across crypto markets and decentralised finance protocols. It supports exchange compliance teams, law enforcement, insolvency practitioners, and researchers who need to follow funds through wallets, smart contracts, and cross-chain bridges. The work covers both public ledgers such as Bitcoin and Ethereum and, where data is available, layer-two networks and sidechains. Its outputs are used in suspicious activity reporting, civil recovery, and market surveillance rather than as standalone proof of wrongdoing.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: On-chain forensics is the practice of examining blockchain transaction records to trace the movement of digital assets, attribute addresses to real-world entities, and reconstruct financial activity across crypto markets and decentralised finance protocols. It supports exchange compliance teams, law enforcement, insolvency practitioners, and researchers who need to follow funds through wallets, smart contracts, and cross-chain bridges. The work covers both public ledgers such as Bitcoin and Ethereum and, where data is available, layer-two networks and sidechains. Its outputs are used in suspicious activity reporting, civil recovery, and market surveillance rather than as standalone proof of wrongdoing.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on full and archive blockchain nodes that provide raw transaction and event data, plus indexers that organise this data into queryable form. Analysts typically combine graph databases for address and transaction relationships with relational stores for entity labels and case metadata. Cloud compute and scheduled pipelines handle the volume of blocks, while some teams run local copies of ledgers to preserve evidence. Machine learning models are deployed as scoring services or batch jobs over features extracted from transaction graphs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts begin by identifying seed addresses from known exchanges, seizures, phishing reports, or on-chain patterns, then expand the graph through direct and indirect transfers. Heuristics such as shared input ownership, deposit address reuse, and behavioural timing are used to cluster addresses that likely belong to the same actor. Supervised classifiers and anomaly detection help flag mixers, tumblers, and laundering patterns, but human review remains central because heuristics can fail. Attribution is recorded with confidence levels and supporting evidence rather than as a binary label.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on data provenance, chain of custody, and the possibility of false attribution when addresses are shared or controlled by custodians. Investigators must document how evidence was collected, which heuristics were applied, and what uncertainty remains, because results may be challenged in court or by affected parties. Privacy is a live concern since public ledgers expose transaction histories, and forensic work can re-identify individuals behind pseudonyms. Compliance teams use these methods within data protection and financial surveillance rules, and they avoid treating a cluster label as proof of a specific person's intent.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time monitoring across multiple chains and layer-two systems, where cross-chain bridges and privacy protocols make tracing harder. AI models are being adapted to detect novel laundering patterns and to score risk on newly deployed smart contracts, but adversarial actors continuously change behaviour. Expect tighter integration with exchange compliance workflows and regulatory reporting, as well as more standardised evidence formats for courts. The main open problems are reliable attribution through privacy-preserving technologies and reducing false positives without missing organised activity.
